extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political science, history, and American government
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length explanatory overview of the composition, procedures, motives, and practical rules governing U.S. national nominating conventions (how delegates are chosen, how nominations and balloting proceed, and what strategic considerations shape candidate selection).

rubrics_metrics.name: State delegate apportionment
rubrics_metrics.description: In the nominating convention each State is allowed twice as many delegates as it has electoral votes (two per senator + one per House member × 2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Delaware and Idaho each have six delegates; New York has seventy-eight. Delegates are chosen by local conventions (two per congressional district and four delegates-at-large for the State). The composition of primaries determines local conventions, which in turn determine the national composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegate alternates
rubrics_metrics.description: Every delegate has an alternate chosen by the local convention at the same time, empowered to replace him if he cannot be present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the delegate is present the alternate is silent; if the delegate is absent the alternate steps into his shoes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of delegates vs. instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Local or State conventions may instruct delegates as to their first choice or subsequent ballots, but a delegate is not absolutely bound to follow his instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delegates sometimes vote against instructions; motives for breaking instructions range from corrupt inducement to reasonable changes of judgment or pressure from party chiefs. How censurable a delegate is depends on circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit Rule versus individual voting
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a State delegation votes solidly (Unit Rule) or by individual delegates is a contested point and varies by party practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Democratic party practice sustains instructions and records the whole State vote for the aspirant favored by the majority (Unit Rule). Republican practice (settled in 1876 and 1880) allows delegates to vote individually even when instructed to cast a solid vote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission of territorial and non-electoral delegates
rubrics_metrics.description: Delegates from Territories, District of Columbia, and transmarine possessions have been admitted to national conventions despite having no electoral votes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justification: sustains party interest and energy in areas where the party is weak. Criticism: permits choices to be influenced by delegates whose votes will not affect the presidential election and who may be of lower calibre and more easily swayed by sordid motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convention timing and site selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventions are held in the summer immediately preceding a presidential election (usually June or July) and are held in large cities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large cities are chosen to obtain adequate hotel accommodation and easy railroad access; historical shift in favoured sites with population centre movements (e.g., from Baltimore/Philadelphia to Chicago, Cincinnati, St. Louis, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening and preliminary procedural steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Business begins with the national committee chairman calling the convention to order, nomination of a temporary chairman, appointment of secretaries/clerks, adoption of rules, and nomination of committees (including credentials and resolutions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The convention typically adjourns until committees can report; the temporary chairman vote can indicate factional strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment of permanent chairman and platform presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: At the next sitting the permanent chairman is appointed, inaugurates proceedings with a speech, and the committee on resolutions presents the platform — a series of resolutions embodying party principles and programme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms are usually drawn to conciliate every section and to treat divisive questions with prudent ambiguity. Delegates may move to strike or amend resolutions, but the committee's practiced form is generally sustained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomination procedure by roll-call
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspirants are nominated by roll-call of the States: when a State is called, a prominent delegate proposes the aspirant in a speech extolling his merits, seconded by others; the roll continues until all aspirants are nominated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Average number of nominations is seven or eight (rarely exceeds twelve). Nominations may also be made later in the convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balloting process and majority thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Balloting proceeds by roll-call with each State announcing how its delegates vote; a candidate elected requires a specified majority which varies by party rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Republican rule an absolute majority of those voting suffices; under Democratic rule a two-thirds majority is required. If no one reaches the required number, ballots are repeated until someone does; some historical nominations took many ballots (e.g., 49th, 53rd, 36th ballots in various years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vice-presidential nomination practice
rubrics_metrics.description: After the presidential nominee is chosen, the convention similarly selects its vice-presidential candidate, typically with less excitement and protraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often a defeated aspirant may be nominated for the vice-presidency as consolation, especially if he retired at a useful moment in favour of the chosen rival.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convention's formal vs. practical authority over voters
rubrics_metrics.description: A convention can recommend its candidates to the party but cannot compel individual voters to support the party nominee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties can brand dissenters as 'Kickers' or 'Bolters' and local organizations can expel them from party lists, but enforcing delegates' post-convention support is controversial; the Ironclad Pledge (1880 Republican) attempted to bind delegates in honour to support the nominee, but later attempts provoked resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ironclad Pledge (example of enforced commitment)
rubrics_metrics.description: A resolution asserting that every member of the convention is bound in honour to support its nominee and that no man should hold his seat who will not agree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: carried at the 1880 Republican convention by 716 to 3; a similar resolution in 1884 was opposed strongly and withdrawn, and some delegates later opposed their party's nominee in the election.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary objective in choosing a candidate — availability
rubrics_metrics.description: The party aims to choose the man most likely to win ('available'), not necessarily the wisest or most upright person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors considered: ability, length of public exposure, oratorical gifts, 'magnetism', family connections, appearance, private life purity, record of integrity, personal enmities, and influence of powerful bosses or newspapers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic value of candidate's home state
rubrics_metrics.description: A candidate's home State is important: a candidate from a large doubtful State is especially valuable because he may swing that State's electoral votes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: California (10 electoral votes), Indiana (15), New York (39) — larger doubtful States are more attractive picks; safe States in party colour matter less.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typology of aspirants: Favourites, Dark Horses, Favourite Sons
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspirants are classed as Favourites (nationally known politicians), Dark Horses (less widely known, respectable, safe fallback choices), and Favourite Sons (popular within their State but little regarded nationally).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favourites are few (rarely more than two or three); Favourite Sons more numerous; Dark Horses can be numerous and may emerge during balloting (historical examples: Garfield in 1880, Pierce in 1852). Characteristics and strategic roles described for each type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motives influencing delegates and managers
rubrics_metrics.description: Four sets of motives act on those directing or voting in a convention: desire to carry a particular aspirant; desire to defeat a particular aspirant; desire for personal gain (trading votes for office); desire to find the candidate giving the party the best chance of victory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These motives mix and vary in strength; forecasting their joint effect requires knowledge and skill; managers exploit them to form coalitions and persuade delegates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-period model of convention proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings are best understood as three periods: (1) transactions preceding the opening (preparations/subsoiling), (2) preliminary business (passing rules/resolutions and delivering nominating speeches), and (3) the balloting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-convention activity includes underground work to secure delegates; during preliminary business committees report and platforms often adopted; balloting is the final decisive stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-convention organization and 'subsoiling'
rubrics_metrics.description: About a year before the election factions and bosses begin work to secure delegates: manipulating primaries and local conventions to obtain delegates favourable to their aspirant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspapers start 'booms' for favourites; delegates are often handpicked; 'untiring underground work' by agents and emissaries determines much of the convention result.

rubrics_metrics.name: In-city convention conduct and managerial tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Once delegates arrive, each large delegation and aspirant faction has headquarters and managers who hold perpetual sessions to count numbers, spread rumours, organize raids on less experienced delegates, and carry out 'ploughing around' to win delegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactics include sending 'missionaries' to bring over individuals, accrediting embassies between delegations for vote-trading, and using bands, parades, and large non-delegate followers to create moral support and publicity. All conducted with decorum to avoid scandal.

rubrics_metrics.name: State delegation internal organization and voting mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: Each State delegation has a chairman who announces how his delegates vote and is expected to keep the delegation together, travel and lodge together, hold meetings during the convention, and occupy a particular place in the hall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the chairman's report is challenged the roll of delegates is called and they vote individually. Delegation meetings excitedly decide courses (especially in large and doubtful States) and are avidly observed by reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolution from mass meetings to representative conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Early conventions were largely mass meetings; later conventions are regularly-constituted representative bodies composed exclusively of delegates elected in their States and bringing credentials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative conventions emerged by mid-19th century; exceptions (e.g., early Republican conventions) sometimes resembled mass meetings where organization was incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical significance of platforms — usually formal, sometimes decisive
rubrics_metrics.description: Platforms are often drafted vaguely and pompously by committees and are usually a matter of form, but in critical moments (e.g., 1860 Charleston, 1896 currency debates, 1908 amendments debate) platform debates can be of great consequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms can lead to major party splits (example: the 1860 Democratic secession at Charleston). Most of the time the platform committee's product is sustained without major change.
